lessons.title: Calculating Cost of Production per Unit
lessons.body: To know if you are making a profit, you must first know exactly how much it costs to produce one jar of peanut butter. This is your cost of production per unit. Start by listing all your direct costs for a batch. For example, to make 20 jars of 500g peanut butter, you might use 10 kg of raw groundnuts at 2,000 XAF per kg = 20,000 XAF. You also need 1 kg of sugar (1,000 XAF), 0.5 kg of salt (500 XAF), and 1 litre of oil (2,000 XAF). Your total ingredient cost is 23,500 XAF. Next, add packaging: 20 jars with lids at 200 XAF each = 4,000 XAF, and labels at 50 XAF each = 1,000 XAF. So packaging costs 5,000 XAF. Now add direct labour: if you pay a helper 1,500 XAF to assist for the day, that's 1,500 XAF. Total direct costs = 23,500 + 5,000 + 1,500 = 30,000 XAF. Divide by 20 jars: 30,000 / 20 = 1,500 XAF per jar. But you also have overheads like electricity, rent, and equipment depreciation. Suppose monthly overheads are 30,000 XAF and you produce 300 jars per month, that's 100 XAF per jar. So your full cost per jar is 1,500 + 100 = 1,600 XAF. Always calculate per batch and per unit. Keep a notebook recording every purchase. Use a simple calculator or phone app. If you produce different sizes, calculate cost per gram or per jar separately. Review your costs every month because prices change. This number is the foundation for setting your price.

lessons.title: Setting a Profitable Selling Price
lessons.body: Once you know your cost per unit, you can set a selling price that covers all costs and gives you a profit. A simple method is cost-plus pricing. Decide on a profit margin. For example, if your cost per jar is 1,600 XAF, you might want a 40% profit margin. Multiply cost by 1.4: 1,600 x 1.4 = 2,240 XAF. Round up to 2,500 XAF for easy pricing. But also check what competitors charge. If similar peanut butter sells for 2,200 XAF, you might price at 2,300 XAF to stay competitive while still making 700 XAF profit per jar (2,300 - 1,600 = 700). That's a 44% markup on cost. However, if your costs are higher, you may need to reduce costs or differentiate your product (e.g., organic, no sugar) to charge more. Consider your target market: in cities, people may pay more for quality; in rural areas, price sensitivity is higher. You can also offer bulk discounts: sell 10 jars for 22,000 XAF instead of 23,000 XAF. Always ensure your price covers variable costs (ingredients, packaging) so you don't lose money on each sale. Test prices: start at a level where you make at least 20-30% profit, then adjust based on sales. Keep records of what you charge and how many you sell. If sales are slow, don't immediately drop price; first try to reduce costs or improve marketing. Remember, profit is not greedâit's what allows you to grow, pay yourself, and reinvest.

lessons.title: Keeping Simple Financial Records: Income and Expenses
lessons.body: You cannot manage money you don't track. Keeping simple records means writing down every income and expense daily. Use a notebook or a free app like Excel or a simple ledger book. Divide pages into two columns: Income (money in) and Expenses (money out). For income, record date, description (e.g., 'sold 10 jars to Mama Jane'), and amount. For expenses, record date, description (e.g., 'bought 5 kg groundnuts'), and amount. At the end of each week, total both columns. Subtract expenses from income to get your profit or loss. For example, week 1: income 25,000 XAF, expenses 18,000 XAF, profit 7,000 XAF. Also keep receipts and invoices in a folder. If you buy on credit, note who you owe and when payment is due. If you sell on credit, note who owes you. Every month, do a summary: total sales, total expenses, and profit. This helps you see trends: are sales increasing? Are certain expenses too high? You can also calculate your break-even point: total fixed costs divided by (selling price - variable cost per unit). For instance, if fixed costs are 30,000 XAF per month, selling price is 2,500 XAF, variable cost per jar is 1,500 XAF, then break-even = 30,000 / (2,500 - 1,500) = 30 jars. So you need to sell at least 30 jars monthly to cover all costs. Simple records also help when applying for loans or grants. Lenders want to see that you are organized. Use a separate bank account for business if possible, or a mobile money wallet. Never mix personal and business money. At the end of each day, count your cash and reconcile with records. This discipline will save you from surprises.

lessons.title: Managing Cash Flow for Small Business
lessons.body: Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of your business. Even if you are profitable on paper, you can run out of cash if you don't manage timing. For example, you might sell 100 jars on credit, expecting payment in 30 days, but you need to buy groundnuts now. If you have no cash, you can't produce. To manage cash flow, follow these steps: First, forecast your cash needs. Look at your monthly expenses: raw materials, packaging, labour, rent, transport. Estimate when you will receive payments from customers. If you sell mostly cash, you have good cash flow. If you sell to shops on credit, you may need a cash buffer. Second, speed up cash inflows: offer a small discount for early payment (e.g., 5% off if paid within 7 days). Third, slow down cash outflows: negotiate with suppliers for credit terms (e.g., pay for groundnuts in 14 days). Buy in bulk when prices are low, but don't tie up all your cash. Fourth, keep a cash reserve for emergencies. Aim to have at least one month's expenses in cash. Fifth, separate business and personal cash. Pay yourself a fixed salary rather than dipping into the till. Use a cash flow spreadsheet: list opening cash, add expected inflows, subtract expected outflows, and see closing cash. If closing cash is negative, you need to adjust: delay purchases, increase sales, or get a short-term loan. For example, if you expect to have 10,000 XAF at month end but need 15,000 XAF for rent, you must find 5,000 XAF. Track your actual cash daily. A simple notebook with columns for date, cash in, cash out, and balance works. Review weekly. Good cash flow management keeps your business alive and stress-free.

lessons.title: Accessing Microfinance and Loans for Expansion
lessons.body: When you want to expandâbuy a bigger grinder, hire more staff, or reach new marketsâyou may need a loan. Microfinance institutions (MFIs) and banks in Africa offer loans to small businesses, but you must prepare. First, know your numbers: have at least 6 months of financial records showing income, expenses, and profit. Lenders want to see that you can repay. Second, decide how much you need and what for. For example, a new grinding machine costs 500,000 XAF. You might save 200,000 XAF and borrow 300,000 XAF. Third, approach MFIs like Kiva, BRAC, or local savings groups (e.g., Village Savings and Loan Associations). They often require collateral, but some accept group guarantees. Interest rates vary: 10-30% per year. Calculate the monthly repayment: for a 300,000 XAF loan at 20% annual interest over 12 months, you pay about 27,500 XAF per month. Ensure your business profit can cover that. Fourth, prepare a simple business plan: describe your product, market, costs, and projected sales. Show how the loan will increase profits. Fifth, build a relationship with the lender: start with a small loan and repay on time to build trust. Avoid borrowing from loan sharks with high interest. Also consider grants from NGOs or government programs for small businesses. Before taking a loan, ask: will this investment generate more income than the cost of the loan? If yes, it's worth it. If not, wait. Always keep loan repayments in your cash flow forecast. And never borrow more than you can repay.

lessons.title: Budgeting for Equipment and Raw Materials
lessons.body: A budget is a plan for how you will spend your money. For a peanut butter business, you need to budget for equipment and raw materials. Start with equipment: list what you have and what you need. For example, a manual grinder costs 50,000 XAF, a roasting pan 10,000 XAF, a sealing machine 80,000 XAF, and jars 200 XAF each. If you need a new sealing machine, save a portion of your profit each month. Say you make 50,000 XAF profit monthly; set aside 20,000 XAF for equipment. In 4 months, you can buy the machine. For raw materials, estimate how much you need based on sales. If you sell 300 jars per month, and each jar uses 0.5 kg groundnuts, you need 150 kg per month. At 2,000 XAF per kg, that's 300,000 XAF monthly. Buy in bulk when prices are low after harvest (e.g., October to December). You might buy 6 months' supply at a discount. But ensure you have storage to prevent aflatoxin. Budget for other materials: sugar, salt, oil, jars, labels. Create a monthly budget: list expected income, then allocate to expenses: raw materials (60%), labour (15%), rent (10%), transport (5%), savings (10%). Stick to it. Use envelopes or separate mobile money wallets for each category. Review your budget monthly: did you overspend? Adjust. If income is lower than expected, cut non-essential expenses. A budget helps you avoid impulse buys and ensures you have money for what matters. It also shows lenders you are serious. Update your budget every season because prices fluctuate.

quiz.q: What is the first step to calculate cost of production per unit?
options: B) List all direct costs for a batch
quiz.explanation: You must know all direct costs (ingredients, packaging, labour) before calculating per unit cost.

quiz.q: If a batch of 20 jars costs 30,000 XAF in direct costs, what is the direct cost per jar?
quiz.explanation: 30,000 divided by 20 equals 1,500 XAF per jar.

quiz.q: What are overheads in production?
options: C) Indirect costs like rent and electricity
quiz.explanation: Overheads are indirect costs not directly tied to each unit, such as rent, utilities, and depreciation.

quiz.q: Why should you review your costs every month?
options: B) Because prices of inputs change
quiz.explanation: Input prices fluctuate, so regular review ensures your cost calculations remain accurate.

quiz.q: What is cost-plus pricing?
options: B) Adding a profit margin to cost per unit
quiz.explanation: Cost-plus pricing means adding a desired profit margin to the total cost per unit.

quiz.q: If cost per jar is 1,600 XAF and you want a 40% profit margin, what is the selling price?
quiz.explanation: 1,600 multiplied by 1.4 equals 2,240 XAF.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check competitor prices?
options: B) To ensure your price is competitive while covering costs
quiz.explanation: Knowing competitor prices helps you set a price that attracts customers while still making a profit.

quiz.q: What is a bulk discount?
options: A) Charging more for large orders
B) Reducing price per unit for large orders
quiz.explanation: Bulk discount means lowering the per-unit price when customers buy in larger quantities.

quiz.q: What is the minimum profit margin recommended in the lesson?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests starting with at least 20-30% profit to ensure sustainability.

quiz.q: What should you do if sales are slow?
options: B) Reduce costs or improve marketing first
quiz.explanation: Before cutting price, try to reduce costs or market better to maintain profit margins.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of keeping financial records?
options: B) To track income and expenses for profit calculation
quiz.explanation: Records help you know your profit, manage cash, and make informed decisions.

quiz.q: In a simple ledger, what two main columns should you have?
quiz.explanation: For a small business, tracking income and expenses is the simplest and most useful method.

quiz.q: What is break-even point?
options: A) When you make a profit
B) When total revenue equals total costs
C) When you sell all stock
quiz.explanation: Break-even is the point where income covers all costs, resulting in zero profit or loss.

quiz.q: If fixed costs are 30,000 XAF, selling price 2,500 XAF, variable cost 1,500 XAF, what is break-even in units?
Why should you keep receipts?
options: B) As proof of expenses for records and loans
quiz.explanation: Receipts provide evidence of expenses, useful for accurate records and loan applications.

quiz.q: What is cash flow?
options: B) Movement of money in and out of business
quiz.explanation: Cash flow refers to the actual timing of cash receipts and payments.

quiz.q: Why can a profitable business run out of cash?
options: A) Because profit is not cash
B) Because of credit sales and timing mismatches
D) Because they don't track sales
quiz.explanation: Profit is accounting, but cash flow depends on when money is received and paid; credit sales can delay cash.

quiz.q: What is one way to speed up cash inflows?
options: A) Offer discounts for early payment
quiz.explanation: Offering a small discount encourages customers to pay sooner, improving cash flow.

quiz.q: How much cash reserve is recommended?
quiz.explanation: Aim to have at least one month's expenses in cash to handle emergencies.

quiz.q: What should you do if your cash flow forecast shows negative closing cash?
options: B) Adjust by delaying purchases or increasing sales
quiz.explanation: Adjusting spending and boosting sales are first steps before seeking loans.

quiz.q: What do microfinance institutions typically require before giving a loan?
options: B) Financial records showing repayment ability
quiz.explanation: Lenders want to see that you can repay, so they ask for financial records.

quiz.q: What is a Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA)?
options: B) A group that saves and lends to members
quiz.explanation: VSLAs are community-based groups where members save and borrow from a common fund.

quiz.q: What should you do before taking a loan?
options: A) Borrow as much as possible
B) Ensure the investment will generate more income than loan cost
quiz.explanation: Only borrow if the investment will increase profits enough to cover loan repayments and grow the business.

quiz.q: What is a budget?
options: B) A plan for spending and saving money
quiz.explanation: A budget is a financial plan that allocates expected income to various expenses and savings.

quiz.q: Why is it important to budget for equipment?
options: B) To save gradually for needed tools
quiz.explanation: Budgeting for equipment means setting aside money regularly to purchase tools without disrupting cash flow.

quiz.q: When is the best time to buy raw materials in bulk?
options: B) After harvest when prices are low
quiz.explanation: Buying after harvest when groundnut prices are low can reduce production costs.

quiz.q: What percentage of income does the lesson suggest for raw materials?
quiz.explanation: The sample budget allocates 60% of income to raw materials.

quiz.q: Why should you use separate envelopes or mobile money wallets for budget categories?
options: B) To ensure you don't overspend in one area
quiz.explanation: Separating funds helps you stick to your budget and prevents using money meant for one expense on another.

quiz.q: What should you do if you overspend in a budget category?
quiz.explanation: Review and adjust your budget monthly to stay on track and avoid repeated overspending.
